title: What might have been
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: Sanskrit has no dedicated past counterfactual, so this module builds one. The frame is L3-M4's own yadi … tarhi with an OPTATIVE IN BOTH HALVES: yadi aham hyaḥ gaccheyam tarhi mama mitram paśyeyam.

The optative in the speaker's cell ends -eyam where L3-M4's third singular ends -et: gacchet becomes gaccheyam, paṭhet becomes paṭheyam. Three verbs carry it here — gaccheyam, paṭheyam, paśyeyam — and no fourth.

syāt is 'would be', the optative of L1-M3's asti, and it is what a supposed verbless sentence needs. The set of this verb, side by side at last: asti one is, staḥ two are, santi many are, astu let it be, syāt would be.

What does NOT open with it, so you know the shape of the hole: every dual and plural optative, the second singular gaccheḥ, the athematic kuryāt that L3-M4 already refused, and the conditional agamiṣyat — the one form that means exactly 'would have gone' and that almost nobody says.

The optative in BOTH halves is the only visible difference between a plan and a regret. L3-M4's yadi bhavān adya gacchati tarhi aham api gacchāmi is a live arrangement; yadi mārgaḥ hrasvaḥ syāt tarhi aham hyaḥ gaccheyam is something that did not happen.

The pastness is LEXICAL, never on the verb. hyaḥ is what makes a counterfactual about yesterday, and a sentence with no time word in it is about whatever the situation is about. Nothing in the verb changes when the day does.

English marks unreality twice, in the auxiliary and in the tense, so a learner builds the condition with the participle: yadi aham hyaḥ gatavān … That is a plain statement that the thing DID happen, and it leaves the second half supposing about a fact.

A regret needs no counterfactual at all, and this is the commoner sentence: mahyam duḥkham asti, yataḥ aham hyaḥ na gatavān — L3-M6's dative frame, L1-M9's yataḥ, and a participle reporting the fact behind the feeling.

The listener's half never takes -eyam. bhavān and bhavatī have taken a third-person verb since L1-M2, so a counterfactual about you uses L3-M4's -et and one about me uses -eyam. That is the whole of the person system here.

na stands in front of the optative exactly as it stands in front of a present: samasyā na syāt, 'there would be no problem'. It never negates the bare noun, and tarhi may still be dropped, as L3-M4 said.

sentences.display: yadi aham hyaḥ gaccheyam tarhi mama mitram paśyeyam.
sentences.script: यदि अहम् ह्यः गच्छेयम् तर्हि मम मित्रम् पश्येयम्।
sentences.cue: If I had gone yesterday, I would have seen my friend.
sentences.literal: if I yesterday would-go then my friend would-see

words.note: L3-M4's 'if'. It opens its clause and takes no ending. What changed here is not yadi but the mood of the two verbs it stands over.
L1-M1's 'I'. It is written once at most: the -eyam on the verb already says who is speaking.
L1-M5's 'yesterday', and in this module it is load-bearing: the verbs carry no tense at all, so this one word is what makes the sentence about the past.

words.cue: I would go · I would have gone
words.note: The optative of L1-M2's gacchati in the SPEAKER's cell: -eyam where L3-M4's gacchet has -et. A row of its own here, pointing back at gacchati, with no edit to L1-M2.
L3-M4's 'then', opening the consequence. It may still be left out, exactly as L3-M4 said, and the counterfactual survives without it.
L1-M1's aham in its 'of me' shape. aham acts, mama owns, mahyam receives.
L2-M2's 'friend', and the word is neuter whoever the friend is. Here it is the object of the seeing and the shape does not change for that either.

words.cue: I would see · I would have seen
words.note: The optative of L2-M4's paśyati in the speaker's cell. Its own row here, pointing back at paśyati. This course writes no third-singular paśyet.

sentences.trap: Nothing in this sentence is past. Both verbs are optatives, hyaḥ is the only word carrying time, and take it away and the same seven words are about today.
sentences.sound: YA-di a-HAM HYAH gach-CHEH-yam TAR-hi MA-ma MI-tram pash-YEH-yam. The eyam at the end of both verbs is two syllables, eh-yam.

variations.display: yadi aham adya gaccheyam tarhi mama mitram paśyeyam.
variations.script: यदि अहम् अद्य गच्छेयम् तर्हि मम मित्रम् पश्येयम्।
variations.cue: If I went today, I would see my friend.
variations.changed: one time word swaps and the sentence stops being about the past — the verbs are untouched, which is the whole lesson

variations.display: yadi aham hyaḥ na gaccheyam tarhi mama mitram na paśyeyam.
variations.script: यदि अहम् ह्यः न गच्छेयम् तर्हि मम मित्रम् न पश्येयम्।
variations.cue: If I had not gone yesterday, I would not have seen my friend.
variations.changed: na enters both halves, in front of the optative exactly as it stands in front of a present

variations.display: yadi aham hyaḥ gaccheyam mama mitram paśyeyam.
variations.script: यदि अहम् ह्यः गच्छेयम् मम मित्रम् पश्येयम्।
variations.cue: If I had gone yesterday, I would have seen my friend.
variations.changed: tarhi is dropped, which L3-M4 already allowed, and the counterfactual is unharmed

mistake.display: yadi aham hyaḥ gatavān tarhi mama mitram paśyeyam.
mistake.why: The condition has been built with the participle gatavān, which is a plain statement that I DID go. A counterfactual needs the optative in BOTH halves; a participle in the first half says the thing happened, and then the second half has nothing left to suppose.

sentences.usage: The everyday shape of a regret. A speaker says it about a missed visit far more often than about anything grand.
sentences.mnemonic: Both halves suppose; only hyaḥ remembers.

sentences.display: yadi aham hyaḥ paṭheyam tarhi mahyam sukham syāt.
sentences.script: यदि अहम् ह्यः पठेयम् तर्हि मह्यम् सुखम् स्यात्।
sentences.cue: If I had studied yesterday, I would be happy.
sentences.literal: if I yesterday would-study then to-me happiness would-be

words.note: L3-M4's 'if'. It opens its clause and takes no ending. What changed here is not yadi but the mood of the two verbs it stands over.
L1-M1's 'I'. It is written once at most: the -eyam on the verb already says who is speaking.
L1-M5's 'yesterday', and in this module it is load-bearing: the verbs carry no tense at all, so this one word is what makes the sentence about the past.

words.cue: I would study · I would have studied
words.note: The optative of L1-M4's paṭhati in the speaker's cell, beside L3-M4's third-singular paṭhet. Its own row here, pointing back at paṭhati.
L3-M4's 'then', opening the consequence. It may still be left out, exactly as L3-M4 said, and the counterfactual survives without it.
L1-M1's aham in its 'to me' shape, the one L3-M6 builds a feeling on: mahyam duḥkham asti is 'I am sad'.
L3-M6's neuter noun, the subject of the second half. It is duḥkham's opposite number and is built the same way.
The optative of L1-M3's asti, and the whole of 'would be'. The set, side by side at last: asti one is, staḥ two are, santi many are, astu let it be, syāt would be.

sentences.trap: syāt is third singular and there is no first-person shape of it in this course. 'I would be happy' is therefore built round mahyam and a neuter noun, as L3-M6 built 'I am happy'.
sentences.sound: YA-di a-HAM HYAH pa-THEH-yam TAR-hi MAH-yam SU-kham SYAAT. The syaat is one syllable, sy together.

variations.display: yadi aham hyaḥ paṭheyam tarhi mahyam duḥkham na syāt.
variations.script: यदि अहम् ह्यः पठेयम् तर्हि मह्यम् दुःखम् न स्यात्।
variations.cue: If I had studied yesterday, I would not be sad.
variations.changed: the consequence is negated and the feeling flips with it; na goes in front of syāt like any other verb

variations.display: yadi bhavatī hyaḥ paṭhet tarhi bhavatyai sukham syāt.
variations.script: यदि भवती ह्यः पठेत् तर्हि भवत्यै सुखम् स्यात्।
variations.cue: If you had studied yesterday, you would be happy.
variations.changed: the person shifts to the listener, so -eyam becomes L3-M4's -et and mahyam becomes L2-M5's bhavatyai

variations.display: yadi aham hyaḥ paṭheyam tarhi kim mahyam sukham syāt?
variations.script: यदि अहम् ह्यः पठेयम् तर्हि किम् मह्यम् सुखम् स्यात्?
variations.cue: If I had studied yesterday, would I be happy?
variations.changed: L1-M2's kim turns the consequence into a yes/no question and the condition is untouched

mistake.display: yadi aham hyaḥ paṭhitavān tarhi mahyam sukham syāt.
mistake.why: paṭhitavān says I did study. Once the first half asserts the past, the second half is not a counterfactual any more but a conclusion drawn from a fact, and syāt in front of a fact reads as a hedge instead of a regret.

sentences.usage: What a student says the evening before a result. The regret is in the shape, not in any word meaning 'sorry'.

sentences.display: yadi mārgaḥ hrasvaḥ syāt tarhi aham hyaḥ gaccheyam.
sentences.script: यदि मार्गः ह्रस्वः स्यात् तर्हि अहम् ह्यः गच्छेयम्।
sentences.cue: If the road had been short, I would have gone yesterday.
sentences.literal: if road short would-be then I yesterday would-go

words.note: L3-M4's 'if'. It opens its clause and takes no ending. What changed here is not yadi but the mood of the two verbs it stands over.
L2-M4's road, in the nominative as the subject of the condition. Nothing about the counterfactual touches a noun's case.
L2-M3's 'short' of a thing, agreeing with mārgaḥ. An adjective in a supposed clause looks exactly like an adjective in a real one.
The optative of L1-M3's asti. Here it is the verb of the CONDITION: a verbless nominal sentence, mārgaḥ hrasvaḥ, needs syāt put into it before it can be supposed.
L3-M4's 'then', opening the consequence. It may still be left out, exactly as L3-M4 said, and the counterfactual survives without it.
L1-M1's 'I'. It is written once at most: the -eyam on the verb already says who is speaking.
L1-M5's 'yesterday', and in this module it is load-bearing: the verbs carry no tense at all, so this one word is what makes the sentence about the past.

words.cue: I would go · I would have gone
words.note: L1-M2's gacchati in the speaker's optative cell. It is the consequence here and the condition in S01 — the cell does not care which half it stands in.

sentences.trap: mārgaḥ hrasvaḥ is a complete sentence with no verb at all. To suppose it rather than assert it you must put syāt in, and that is the one place this course ever needs a copula.
sentences.sound: YA-di MAAR-gah HRAS-vah SYAAT TAR-hi a-HAM HYAH gach-CHEH-yam.

variations.display: yadi mārgaḥ dīrghaḥ na syāt tarhi aham hyaḥ gaccheyam.
variations.script: यदि मार्गः दीर्घः न स्यात् तर्हि अहम् ह्यः गच्छेयम्।
variations.cue: If the road had not been long, I would have gone yesterday.
variations.changed: the negation moves into the condition and the adjective flips with it — two ways of saying one thing

variations.display: yadi mārgaḥ hrasvaḥ syāt tarhi bhavān api hyaḥ gacchet.
variations.script: यदि मार्गः ह्रस्वः स्यात् तर्हि भवान् अपि ह्यः गच्छेत्।
variations.cue: If the road had been short, you too would have gone yesterday.
variations.changed: the person shifts to the listener, so the optative moves to L3-M4's -et cell and L1-M10's api comes in behind bhavān

variations.display: mārgaḥ dīrghaḥ, ataḥ aham hyaḥ na gatavān.
variations.script: मार्गः दीर्घः, अतः अहम् ह्यः न गतवान्।
variations.cue: The road is long, so I did not go yesterday.
variations.changed: the supposition becomes a report: L1-M9's ataḥ and L1-M2's participle, with no optative anywhere

mistake.display: yadi mārgaḥ hrasvaḥ tarhi aham hyaḥ gaccheyam.
mistake.why: The condition has been left verbless. mārgaḥ hrasvaḥ asserts that the road IS short, so the sentence says 'the road is short, so I would have gone', which is not a counterfactual. The supposition needs syāt.

sentences.usage: The half a speaker most often reaches for when explaining a decision already taken.
sentences.mnemonic: To suppose a verbless sentence, give it syāt.

sentences.display: yadi bhavān hyaḥ alpam khādet tarhi adya bhavān kuśalī syāt.
sentences.script: यदि भवान् ह्यः अल्पम् खादेत् तर्हि अद्य भवान् कुशली स्यात्।
sentences.cue: If you had eaten a little yesterday, you would be well today.
sentences.literal: if you yesterday a-little would-eat then today you well would-be

words.note: L3-M4's 'if'. It opens its clause and takes no ending. What changed here is not yadi but the mood of the two verbs it stands over.
L1-M2's polite 'you', with a THIRD-person verb after it. That is why the listener's half of a counterfactual uses -et and never -eyam.
L1-M5's 'yesterday', and in this module it is load-bearing: the verbs carry no tense at all, so this one word is what makes the sentence about the past.
L2-M9's 'a little', standing in front of the verb it measures. L3-M4 put it in front of khādet in exactly this slot.
L3-M4's optative of khādati, reused with no new row. It is one of the three -et cells this course has, and there are no others.
L3-M4's 'then', opening the consequence. It may still be left out, exactly as L3-M4 said, and the counterfactual survives without it.
L1-M4's 'today'. A counterfactual about yesterday can have its consequence in today, and the time words say which half is when.
L1-M2's polite 'you' again, in the second half. It is written twice here because the two clauses have different times and the sentence reads more clearly with the subject in both.
L1-M2's 'well', of a man. It would be kuśalinī of a woman, and syāt would not change.
L1-M3's asti in the optative. bhavān kuśalī is a verbless sentence; syāt is what turns it into something supposed rather than reported.

sentences.trap: The listener's half never takes -eyam. bhavān is followed by a third-person verb everywhere in this course, so a counterfactual about you uses L3-M4's -et and a counterfactual about me uses -eyam.
sentences.sound: YA-di bha-VAAN HYAH AL-pam KHAA-det TAR-hi A-dya bha-VAAN ku-sha-LEE SYAAT.

variations.display: yadi bhavatī hyaḥ alpam khādet tarhi adya bhavatī kuśalinī syāt.
variations.script: यदि भवती ह्यः अल्पम् खादेत् तर्हि अद्य भवती कुशलिनी स्यात्।
variations.cue: If you had eaten a little yesterday, you would be well today.
variations.changed: the listener is a woman: bhavatī and kuśalinī fork, and neither khādet nor syāt moves

variations.display: yadi bhavān hyaḥ adhikam na khādet tarhi adya bhavān kuśalī syāt.
variations.script: यदि भवान् ह्यः अधिकम् न खादेत् तर्हि अद्य भवान् कुशली स्यात्।
variations.cue: If you had not eaten too much yesterday, you would be well today.
variations.changed: L2-M9's adhikam replaces alpam and na negates the condition — the same advice from the other end

variations.display: kim bhavān hyaḥ alpam khāditavān?
variations.script: किम् भवान् ह्यः अल्पम् खादितवान्?
variations.cue: Did you eat a little yesterday?
variations.changed: the whole supposition collapses into L1-M2's kim question in the plain participial past

mistake.display: yadi bhavān hyaḥ alpam khādeyam tarhi adya bhavān kuśalī syāt.
mistake.why: -eyam is the SPEAKER's ending and bhavān is the listener. The two cannot meet. Beside that, khādeyam is not a form this course writes at all: the -eyam cells here are gaccheyam, paṭheyam and paśyeyam and there is no fourth.

sentences.usage: Advice one day too late. A speaker softens it further by dropping hyaḥ, which turns the regret into standing advice.

sentences.display: yadi aham hyaḥ patram paśyeyam tarhi samasyā na syāt.
sentences.script: यदि अहम् ह्यः पत्रम् पश्येयम् तर्हि समस्या न स्यात्।
sentences.cue: If I had seen the letter yesterday, there would be no problem.
sentences.literal: if I yesterday letter would-see then problem not would-be

words.note: L3-M4's 'if'. It opens its clause and takes no ending. What changed here is not yadi but the mood of the two verbs it stands over.
L1-M1's 'I'. It is written once at most: the -eyam on the verb already says who is speaking.
L1-M5's 'yesterday', and in this module it is load-bearing: the verbs carry no tense at all, so this one word is what makes the sentence about the past.
L3-M8's wide word for a written sheet. It is the object of the seeing and takes the same shape it takes as a subject, because it is neuter.

words.cue: I would see · I would have seen
words.note: L2-M4's paśyati in the speaker's optative cell. Seeing is what a regret is usually about, which is why this is one of the three verbs the cell opens on.
L3-M4's 'then', opening the consequence. It may still be left out, exactly as L3-M4 said, and the counterfactual survives without it.
L2-M8's 'problem', feminine and in the nominative. It is the subject of syāt, and a subject's case is untouched by the mood of its verb.
L1-M2's 'not', standing in front of the verb it negates. An optative is negated exactly like a present.
L1-M3's asti in the optative. samasyā na syāt is 'there would be no problem' — the existence is supposed and then denied.

sentences.trap: na goes in front of syāt and not in front of samasyā. L1-M2's rule is unchanged: na negates a verb, never a bare noun.
sentences.sound: YA-di a-HAM HYAH PA-tram pash-YEH-yam TAR-hi sa-mas-YAA NA SYAAT.

variations.display: yadi aham adya patram paśyeyam tarhi samasyā na syāt.
variations.script: यदि अहम् अद्य पत्रम् पश्येयम् तर्हि समस्या न स्यात्।
variations.cue: If I saw the letter today, there would be no problem.
variations.changed: hyaḥ gives way to adya and the impossible condition becomes an open one, with no verb changing

variations.display: yadi aham hyaḥ patram na paśyeyam tarhi samasyā syāt.
variations.script: यदि अहम् ह्यः पत्रम् न पश्येयम् तर्हि समस्या स्यात्।
variations.cue: If I had not seen the letter yesterday, there would be a problem.
variations.changed: the negation moves from the consequence into the condition and the consequence turns positive

variations.display: mahyam duḥkham asti, yataḥ aham hyaḥ patram na paṭhitavān.
variations.script: मह्यम् दुःखम् अस्ति, यतः अहम् ह्यः पत्रम् न पठितवान्।
variations.cue: I am sad, because I did not read the letter yesterday.
variations.changed: the same regret rebuilt with no supposition at all — L3-M6's dative frame, L1-M9's yataḥ and a participle

mistake.display: yadi aham hyaḥ patram paśyeyam tarhi na samasyā syāt.
mistake.why: na has been put in front of the noun. Sanskrit negates the verb: samasyā na syāt. na samasyā would have to mean something like 'a non-problem', which is not what the sentence is for.

sentences.usage: An office sentence. The letter is patram, the trouble is samasyā, and the supposition is the polite half of an apology.
sentences.mnemonic: Negate the verb, never the noun.

sentences.display: mahyam duḥkham asti, yataḥ aham hyaḥ na gatavān.
sentences.script: मह्यम् दुःखम् अस्ति, यतः अहम् ह्यः न गतवान्।
sentences.cue: I am sad, because I did not go yesterday.
sentences.literal: to-me sorrow is, because I yesterday not went

words.note: L1-M1's aham in its 'to me' shape, the one L3-M6 builds a feeling on: mahyam duḥkham asti is 'I am sad'.
L3-M6's neuter noun. With mahyam in front of it, it is the whole of 'I am sad' — no adjective and no first-person verb.
L1-M3's 'is'. It states a fact about now; syāt is the same verb supposing instead of stating.
L1-M9's 'because', heading the cause. L4-M2 settled where it may stand; one link takes this marker or ataḥ, never both.
L1-M1's 'I'. It is written once at most: the -eyam on the verb already says who is speaking.
L1-M5's 'yesterday', and in this module it is load-bearing: the verbs carry no tense at all, so this one word is what makes the sentence about the past.
L1-M2's 'not', standing in front of the verb it negates. An optative is negated exactly like a present.
L1-M2's participial past, forking with the speaker. This clause REPORTS the past rather than supposing it, which is why there is no optative in the sentence.

sentences.trap: There is no counterfactual here at all. A regret does not require one: the feeling is stated and the fact behind it is reported, and this is what a speaker says most of the time.
sentences.sound: MAH-yam DUH-kham AS-ti, ya-TAH a-HAM HYAH NA ga-ta-VAAN.

variations.display: mahyam duḥkham asti, yataḥ sā hyaḥ na gatavatī.
variations.script: मह्यम् दुःखम् अस्ति, यतः सा ह्यः न गतवती।
variations.cue: I am sad, because she did not go yesterday.
variations.changed: the cause is about somebody else, so the participle forks to gatavatī while the feeling stays with mahyam

variations.display: aham hyaḥ na gatavān, ataḥ mahyam duḥkham asti.
variations.script: अहम् ह्यः न गतवान्, अतः मह्यम् दुःखम् अस्ति।
variations.cue: I did not go yesterday, so I am sad.
variations.changed: the link is marked at the other end — L1-M9's ataḥ on the consequence instead of yataḥ on the cause

variations.display: yadi aham hyaḥ gaccheyam tarhi mahyam duḥkham na syāt.
variations.script: यदि अहम् ह्यः गच्छेयम् तर्हि मह्यम् दुःखम् न स्यात्।
variations.cue: If I had gone yesterday, I would not be sad.
variations.changed: the same regret rebuilt as a counterfactual: two optatives arrive and both the participle and the connective leave

mistake.display: mahyam duḥkham asti, yataḥ aham hyaḥ na gaccheyam.
mistake.why: An optative in a yataḥ clause supposes the cause instead of stating it, so the sentence says 'I am sad because I would not go', which explains nothing. A reason is a fact, and a fact takes the participle.

sentences.usage: The plainest regret in the language, and the one to reach for first. The counterfactual is for when the missed thing itself has to be named.
sentences.mnemonic: Reasons are facts; facts take the participle.

sentences.display: yadi bhavatī hyaḥ idam pustakam paṭhet tarhi adya samasyā na syāt.
sentences.script: यदि भवती ह्यः इदम् पुस्तकम् पठेत् तर्हि अद्य समस्या न स्यात्।
sentences.cue: If you had read this book yesterday, there would be no problem today.
sentences.literal: if you yesterday this book would-read then today problem not would-be

words.note: L3-M4's 'if'. It opens its clause and takes no ending. What changed here is not yadi but the mood of the two verbs it stands over.
L1-M2's polite 'you' to a woman. The verb does not fork for it — only an adjective does.
L1-M5's 'yesterday', and in this module it is load-bearing: the verbs carry no tense at all, so this one word is what makes the sentence about the past.
L1-M1's neuter 'this', leaning on pustakam. It is the pointing word this course uses; L3-M2's tat is a correlative and does a different job.
L1-M1's book, the object of the reading. Neuter, so subject and object look alike.
L3-M4's optative of paṭhati, reused with no new row. Beside it stands this module's paṭheyam, the same cell in the speaker's person.
L3-M4's 'then', opening the consequence. It may still be left out, exactly as L3-M4 said, and the counterfactual survives without it.
L1-M4's 'today'. A counterfactual about yesterday can have its consequence in today, and the time words say which half is when.
L2-M8's 'problem'. The two halves sit in different times — yesterday's reading, today's trouble — and only the time words say so.
L1-M2's 'not', standing in front of the verb it negates. An optative is negated exactly like a present.
L1-M3's asti in the optative, carrying the whole of 'there would be'.

sentences.trap: The two halves are in different times and no verb says so. hyaḥ and adya carry the whole of it, which is exactly the arrangement this module exists to teach.
sentences.sound: YA-di bha-va-TEE HYAH i-DAM PUS-ta-kam PA-thet TAR-hi A-dya sa-mas-YAA NA SYAAT.

variations.display: yadi aham hyaḥ idam pustakam paṭheyam tarhi adya samasyā na syāt.
variations.script: यदि अहम् ह्यः इदम् पुस्तकम् पठेयम् तर्हि अद्य समस्या न स्यात्।
variations.cue: If I had read this book yesterday, there would be no problem today.
variations.changed: the person shifts to the speaker and the optative moves from the -et cell to the -eyam one; nothing else in the sentence knows

variations.display: yadi bhavatī hyaḥ idam pustakam na paṭhet tarhi adya samasyā syāt.
variations.script: यदि भवती ह्यः इदम् पुस्तकम् न पठेत् तर्हि अद्य समस्या स्यात्।
variations.cue: If you had not read this book yesterday, there would be a problem today.
variations.changed: the na moves from the consequence into the condition and both halves turn over

variations.display: kim bhavatī hyaḥ idam pustakam paṭhitavatī?
variations.script: किम् भवती ह्यः इदम् पुस्तकम् पठितवती?
variations.cue: Did you read this book yesterday?
variations.changed: the supposition becomes a plain question in the participial past, forked to a woman

mistake.display: yadi bhavatī hyaḥ idam pustakam paṭhitavatī tarhi adya samasyā na syāt.
mistake.why: The participle in the condition says you DID read it. The sentence then means 'since you read this book yesterday, there would be no problem today', which contradicts itself: the trouble is here precisely because the reading did not happen.

sentences.usage: What a colleague says about a briefing nobody opened. The politeness lives in bhavatī, not in the mood.
sentences.mnemonic: Two optatives, two time words, two different days.

sentences.display: yadi hyaḥ vṛṣṭiḥ na syāt tarhi aham mandiram gaccheyam.
sentences.script: यदि ह्यः वृष्टिः न स्यात् तर्हि अहम् मन्दिरम् गच्छेयम्।
sentences.cue: If it had not rained yesterday, I would have gone to the temple.
sentences.literal: if yesterday rain not would-be then I temple would-go

words.note: L3-M4's 'if'. It opens its clause and takes no ending. What changed here is not yadi but the mood of the two verbs it stands over.
L1-M5's 'yesterday', and in this module it is load-bearing: the verbs carry no tense at all, so this one word is what makes the sentence about the past.
L4-M2's rain in its citation shape, as the subject. L4-M2's own sentences use the ablative vṛṣṭeḥ for the cause; here the rain is what is being supposed away, so it is a subject.
L1-M2's 'not', standing in front of the verb it negates. An optative is negated exactly like a present.
L1-M3's asti in the optative. vṛṣṭiḥ na syāt is 'there would be no rain' — the same existential asti L1-M3 opened, supposed instead of stated.
L3-M4's 'then', opening the consequence. It may still be left out, exactly as L3-M4 said, and the counterfactual survives without it.
L1-M1's 'I'. It is written once at most: the -eyam on the verb already says who is speaking.
L3-M9's temple, as the place gone to. It is neuter, so the destination looks like the subject would.

words.cue: I would go · I would have gone
words.note: L1-M2's gacchati in the speaker's optative cell, carrying the trip that did not happen.

sentences.trap: The rain is a subject here, not a cause. L4-M2's vṛṣṭeḥ would say 'because of the rain' and would leave nothing for the condition to suppose.
sentences.sound: YA-di HYAH VRISH-tih NA SYAAT TAR-hi a-HAM MAN-di-ram gach-CHEH-yam.

variations.display: yadi adya vṛṣṭiḥ na syāt tarhi aham mandiram gaccheyam.
variations.script: यदि अद्य वृष्टिः न स्यात् तर्हि अहम् मन्दिरम् गच्छेयम्।
variations.cue: If it were not raining today, I would go to the temple.
variations.changed: the time word moves to today and the impossible condition becomes a live one — the rain is still falling either way

variations.display: vṛṣṭeḥ aham hyaḥ mandiram na gatavān.
variations.script: वृष्टेः अहम् ह्यः मन्दिरम् न गतवान्।
variations.cue: Because of the rain I did not go to the temple yesterday.
variations.changed: the supposition collapses into L4-M2's cause ablative and a participle: one word for the reason, no optative at all

variations.display: yadi hyaḥ vṛṣṭiḥ na syāt tarhi bhavān api mandiram gacchet.
variations.script: यदि ह्यः वृष्टिः न स्यात् तर्हि भवान् अपि मन्दिरम् गच्छेत्।
variations.cue: If it had not rained yesterday, you too would have gone to the temple.
variations.changed: the person shifts to the listener, so -eyam becomes -et and L1-M10's api sits behind bhavān

mistake.display: yadi hyaḥ vṛṣṭeḥ na syāt tarhi aham mandiram gaccheyam.
mistake.why: vṛṣṭeḥ is the ablative and already means 'because of the rain', so the condition reads 'if there would not be because-of-the-rain'. A thing being supposed away is the SUBJECT of syāt and takes the nominative vṛṣṭiḥ.

sentences.usage: Weather is the commonest thing to suppose away, in Sanskrit as anywhere. This and L4-M2's vṛṣṭeḥ sentence are the two halves of the same complaint.
sentences.mnemonic: Suppose it away and it is a subject.

sentences.display: yadi bhavān hyaḥ gṛham gacchet tarhi bhavataḥ mātā santuṣṭā syāt.
sentences.script: यदि भवान् ह्यः गृहम् गच्छेत् तर्हि भवतः माता सन्तुष्टा स्यात्।
sentences.cue: If you had gone home yesterday, your mother would be content.
sentences.literal: if you yesterday home would-go then of-you mother content would-be

words.note: L3-M4's 'if'. It opens its clause and takes no ending. What changed here is not yadi but the mood of the two verbs it stands over.
L1-M2's polite 'you', with a THIRD-person verb after it. That is why the listener's half of a counterfactual uses -et and never -eyam.
L1-M5's 'yesterday', and in this module it is load-bearing: the verbs carry no tense at all, so this one word is what makes the sentence about the past.
L1-M6's home, as the place gone to. Neuter, and unchanged by the mood of the verb after it.
L3-M4's optative of gacchati, reused with no new row. It is the listener's cell; this module's gaccheyam is the speaker's.
L3-M4's 'then', opening the consequence. It may still be left out, exactly as L3-M4 said, and the counterfactual survives without it.
L1-M2's bhavān in its 'of you' shape, to a man. To a woman it is bhavatyāḥ, and mātā would not move.
L2-M2's mother, the subject of the second half. She is content or not; the supposing is done by syāt alone.
L1-M9's santuṣṭaḥ forked to a woman. An adjective agrees with who it describes even inside something only supposed.
L1-M3's asti in the optative. mātā santuṣṭā is a complete verbless sentence; syāt is what makes it supposed.

sentences.trap: Two people are in this sentence and only one of them is being advised. The optative on gacchet is about the listener; syāt is about the mother, and both are third singular.
sentences.sound: YA-di bha-VAAN HYAH GRI-ham GACH-chet TAR-hi bha-va-TAH MAA-taa san-tush-TAA SYAAT.

variations.display: yadi bhavatī hyaḥ gṛham gacchet tarhi bhavatyāḥ mātā santuṣṭā syāt.
variations.script: यदि भवती ह्यः गृहम् गच्छेत् तर्हि भवत्याः माता सन्तुष्टा स्यात्।
variations.cue: If you had gone home yesterday, your mother would be content.
variations.changed: the listener is a woman, so bhavataḥ becomes bhavatyāḥ; the verbs do not fork, because this course never forks a verb for gender

variations.display: yadi aham hyaḥ gṛham gaccheyam tarhi mama mātā santuṣṭā syāt.
variations.script: यदि अहम् ह्यः गृहम् गच्छेयम् तर्हि मम माता सन्तुष्टा स्यात्।
variations.cue: If I had gone home yesterday, my mother would be content.
variations.changed: the person shifts to the speaker: gacchet becomes gaccheyam and bhavataḥ becomes L1-M1's mama

variations.display: bhavān hyaḥ gṛham na gatavān, ataḥ bhavataḥ mātā khinnā.
variations.script: भवान् ह्यः गृहम् न गतवान्, अतः भवतः माता खिन्ना।
variations.cue: You did not go home yesterday, so your mother is unhappy.
variations.changed: the supposition becomes a report: L1-M2's participle, L1-M9's ataḥ, and a verbless present for the feeling

mistake.display: yadi bhavān hyaḥ gṛham gaccheyam tarhi bhavataḥ mātā santuṣṭā syāt.
mistake.why: gaccheyam is the speaker's ending sitting after bhavān. The listener always takes a third-person verb in this course, so the cell here is L3-M4's gacchet — and the two endings are a level apart precisely so they are never swapped.

sentences.usage: A reproach with the sting taken out. Putting the consequence on somebody absent is what makes it bearable.
sentences.mnemonic: One supposing sentence can hold two people.

sentences.display: yadi aham adhikam paṭheyam tarhi pariṇāmaḥ uttamaḥ syāt.
sentences.script: यदि अहम् अधिकम् पठेयम् तर्हि परिणामः उत्तमः स्यात्।
sentences.cue: If I had studied more, the result would have been excellent.
sentences.literal: if I more would-study then result excellent would-be

words.note: L3-M4's 'if'. It opens its clause and takes no ending. What changed here is not yadi but the mood of the two verbs it stands over.
L1-M1's 'I'. It is written once at most: the -eyam on the verb already says who is speaking.
L2-M9's 'more', in front of the verb it measures. It says how much of the studying, not how much of anything else.

words.cue: I would study · I would have studied
words.note: L1-M4's paṭhati in the speaker's optative cell. Its own row here, pointing back at paṭhati, because a level never edits a file below it.
L3-M4's 'then', opening the consequence. It may still be left out, exactly as L3-M4 said, and the counterfactual survives without it.
L4-M2's 'result', a row opened one rung ago precisely so phalam could keep meaning fruit. Here it is the subject of syāt.
L2-M3's warm praise, agreeing with pariṇāmaḥ. The praise is being supposed, not given.
L1-M3's asti in the optative, closing the sentence. pariṇāmaḥ uttamaḥ would be a flat claim; syāt makes it a thing that did not happen.

sentences.trap: There is no time word in this sentence and it is still a regret. The situation carries the pastness on its own — which is also why adding hyaḥ narrows it to one particular day.
sentences.sound: YA-di a-HAM A-dhi-kam pa-THEH-yam TAR-hi pa-ri-NAA-mah ut-ta-MAH SYAAT.

variations.display: yadi aham hyaḥ adhikam paṭheyam tarhi pariṇāmaḥ uttamaḥ syāt.
variations.script: यदि अहम् ह्यः अधिकम् पठेयम् तर्हि परिणामः उत्तमः स्यात्।
variations.cue: If I had studied more yesterday, the result would have been excellent.
variations.changed: hyaḥ is added and the regret is pinned to one day instead of to a whole term

variations.display: yadi aham alpam paṭheyam tarhi pariṇāmaḥ uttamaḥ na syāt.
variations.script: यदि अहम् अल्पम् पठेयम् तर्हि परिणामः उत्तमः न स्यात्।
variations.cue: If I had studied little, the result would not have been excellent.
variations.changed: L2-M9's alpam replaces adhikam and na enters the consequence — the scale turns and the outcome turns with it

variations.display: aham adhikam na paṭhitavān, ataḥ pariṇāmaḥ na uttamaḥ.
variations.script: अहम् अधिकम् न पठितवान्, अतः परिणामः न उत्तमः।
variations.cue: I did not study more, so the result is not good.
variations.changed: the whole supposition becomes a report: a participle, L1-M9's ataḥ, and a verbless present

mistake.display: yadi aham adhikam paṭheyam tarhi pariṇāmaḥ uttamaḥ.
mistake.why: The consequence has been left verbless, so it asserts: 'the result IS excellent'. A verbless sentence in Sanskrit is a claim about now, and the moment one half of a counterfactual asserts, the sentence stops supposing. syāt is what the second half needs.

sentences.usage: Said after a result is out. Without hyaḥ it is about a habit rather than a day, which is usually the honest version.
sentences.mnemonic: No time word, and still yesterday.

comprehensionPool.display: yadi aham hyaḥ vidyālayam gaccheyam tarhi saṃskṛtam paṭheyam.
comprehensionPool.script: यदि अहम् ह्यः विद्यालयम् गच्छेयम् तर्हि संस्कृतम् पठेयम्।
comprehensionPool.cue: If I had gone to school yesterday, I would have studied Sanskrit.

comprehensionPool.display: yadi bhavān hyaḥ mandiram gacchet tarhi bhavān santuṣṭaḥ syāt.
comprehensionPool.script: यदि भवान् ह्यः मन्दिरम् गच्छेत् तर्हि भवान् सन्तुष्टः स्यात्।
comprehensionPool.cue: If you had gone to the temple yesterday, you would be content.

comprehensionPool.display: mahyam duḥkham asti, yataḥ saḥ hyaḥ na uktavān.
comprehensionPool.script: मह्यम् दुःखम् अस्ति, यतः सः ह्यः न उक्तवान्।
comprehensionPool.cue: I am sad, because he did not speak yesterday.

comprehensionPool.display: yadi mama pustakam atra syāt tarhi aham paṭheyam.
comprehensionPool.script: यदि मम पुस्तकम् अत्र स्यात् तर्हि अहम् पठेयम्।
comprehensionPool.cue: If my book were here, I would read it.

comprehensionPool.display: yadi vṛṣṭiḥ na syāt tarhi mārgaḥ uttamaḥ syāt.
comprehensionPool.script: यदि वृष्टिः न स्यात् तर्हि मार्गः उत्तमः स्यात्।
comprehensionPool.cue: If it were not raining, the road would be good.

comprehensionPool.display: yadi bhavatī alpam khādet tarhi bhavatī kuśalinī syāt.
comprehensionPool.script: यदि भवती अल्पम् खादेत् तर्हि भवती कुशलिनी स्यात्।
comprehensionPool.cue: If you ate a little, you would be well.

comprehensionPool.display: aham hyaḥ na paṭhitavān, ataḥ mahyam adya cintā asti.
comprehensionPool.script: अहम् ह्यः न पठितवान्, अतः मह्यम् अद्य चिन्ता अस्ति।
comprehensionPool.cue: I did not study yesterday, so I am worried today.

comprehensionPool.display: yadi aham hyaḥ kāryālayam gaccheyam tarhi patram paśyeyam.
comprehensionPool.script: यदि अहम् ह्यः कार्यालयम् गच्छेयम् तर्हि पत्रम् पश्येयम्।
comprehensionPool.cue: If I had gone to the office yesterday, I would have seen the letter.

comprehensionPool.display: yadi saḥ hyaḥ mama gṛham gacchet tarhi mahyam sukham syāt.
comprehensionPool.script: यदि सः ह्यः मम गृहम् गच्छेत् तर्हि मह्यम् सुखम् स्यात्।
comprehensionPool.cue: If he had come to my house yesterday, I would be happy.

comprehensionPool.display: yadi adhyāpakaḥ atra syāt tarhi samasyā na syāt.
comprehensionPool.script: यदि अध्यापकः अत्र स्यात् तर्हि समस्या न स्यात्।
comprehensionPool.cue: If the teacher were here, there would be no problem.

comprehensionPool.display: vṛṣṭeḥ aham hyaḥ na gatavān, ataḥ mahyam duḥkham asti.
comprehensionPool.script: वृष्टेः अहम् ह्यः न गतवान्, अतः मह्यम् दुःखम् अस्ति।
comprehensionPool.cue: Because of the rain I did not go yesterday, so I am sad.

comprehensionPool.display: yadi bhavatyāḥ mātā atra syāt tarhi bhavatī santuṣṭā syāt.
comprehensionPool.script: यदि भवत्याः माता अत्र स्यात् तर्हि भवती सन्तुष्टा स्यात्।
comprehensionPool.cue: If your mother were here, you would be content.

comprehensionPool.display: yadi mama mitram atra syāt tarhi aham na khinnaḥ.
comprehensionPool.script: यदि मम मित्रम् अत्र स्यात् तर्हि अहम् न खिन्नः।
comprehensionPool.cue: If my friend were here, I would not be unhappy.
